title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
pattern: Preorder with markers for empty spots
statement: Design `serialize`, which turns a binary tree into a string, and `deserialize`, which rebuilds exactly the same tree from that string.

example.why: Writing None for every empty spot records the shape, so the string can be read back without guessing.

picture: Picture writing a tree down as a list of instructions for rebuilding it, top first: each node's value, then its whole left side, then its whole right side, with *None* wherever a child is missing. Rebuilding just reads the list in the same order: each value makes a node, and a *None* says *nothing here, go back up*. Because the empty spots are written down too, the shape comes back exactly.
idea: A plain list of values is not enough — many different trees contain the same values. The **shape** has to be stored too.
Write the tree in preorder (node, then left subtree, then right subtree) and write `None` for every empty spot. With those markers the text describes exactly one tree.
To rebuild, read the tokens in the same order: a value creates a node and is followed by its left subtree and then its right subtree; a `None` means *nothing here*.

say.1: The problem asks for a class called `Codec` with two functions, `serialize` and `deserialize`.
say.2: The first function: turn the tree under `root` into one string.
say.3: The pieces of the string, in order.
say.5: A helper that writes a node, then its left side, then its right side.
say.7: Write `None`, so the rebuild knows a child is missing here.
say.9: Write this node's value as text.
say.10: Then write its whole left side (the helper calls itself).
say.13: Write the whole tree, starting from the top.
say.14: Join the pieces with commas into one string.
say.16: The second function: turn such a string back into a tree.
say.17: Cut the string at the commas, back into its pieces.
say.18: The position of the next piece to read.
say.20: A helper that reads the next pieces and builds the subtree they describe.
say.21: Let the helper move `pos`, which belongs to the outer function.
say.25: Then there is no node here.
say.27: Otherwise make a node holding that number.
say.28: The pieces that follow describe its left side: build it (the helper calls itself).
say.29: Then the pieces after those describe its right side.
say.30: This node and both its sides are rebuilt: return it.
say.32: Rebuild the whole tree, starting from the first piece.

complexity.timeWhy: Each node (and each empty spot) is written once and read once; the tokens are joined in a single pass.
complexity.spaceWhy: The string and the token list are proportional to the size of the tree.
